extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (metaphysics, Schopenhauer)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Schopenhauer's methodological and conceptual criteria for recognising the 'will' as the thing-in-itself and for distinguishing will from its phenomenal manifestations (ideas, motives, stimuli, causes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Double knowledge of the body
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of us has a double knowledge of the nature and activity of his own body, 'given in two completely different ways' (as idea and as immediate knowledge of willing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the twofold self-knowledge of one's body as the key analogy: because we know our bodies both as idea and as immediate willing, we may judge other objects (not our bodies) by analogy and infer their inner nature to be will as well. The text: 'The double knowledge which each of us has of the nature and activity of his own body... has now been clearly brought out.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute inner nature of material world to will
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging objects that are not our own bodies (given only as ideas), assume that besides being idea they have an inner nature identical to what we immediately know in ourselves as 'will'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: 'If we wish to attribute the greatest known reality to the material world... we give it the reality which our own body has for each of us; for that is the most real thing for every one.' Therefore, beyond phenomenal appearance, posit will as the thing-in-itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the human will as the paradigmatic manifestation
rubrics_metrics.description: To think the thing-in-itself (which is never object) borrow its name and concept from its most complete manifestation — the human will — and extend this concept to weaker manifestations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological instruction: 'we must borrow for it the name... the most complete of all its manifestations, i.e. the most distinct... the human will.' Warning: avoid misunderstanding by those who limit 'will' to rational, motive-guided phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will proclaims itself in voluntary movements
rubrics_metrics.description: The will primarily declares itself in the voluntary movements of our body; voluntary movements are the visible aspect of individual acts of will and are directly coincident and identical with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use voluntary bodily movements as the immediate evidence for will: 'every voluntary motion... is the manifestation of an act of will.' This provides the empirical starting point for attributing will elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motives determine only temporal/spatial manifestation
rubrics_metrics.description: Motives (ideas) never determine more than what one wills at a particular time and place; they explain the manifestation but not the inner nature of the will itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual rule: 'they merely determine its manifestation at a given point of time... the will itself lies outside the province of the law of motivation, which determines nothing but its appearance at each point of time.' Hence inner will is 'groundless' in the sense of not being explained by sufficient reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish will itself from its manifestations
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate conceptually the inmost essence (will as thing-in-itself) from its many grades of manifestation (accompanied by knowledge, determined by motives, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic practice: identify what 'does not belong to [the will] but to its manifestation' (knowledge, motive-determination). This distinction recurs as method throughout the discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body as objectification of will
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole body must be the manifestation (objectification) of the will — 'my body become visible' — and particular bodily parts correspond to particular desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inference: because every action of the body is manifestation of will and impressions on body affect will (pain/pleasure), conclude body is the will's phenomenal object. Teleological detail: e.g., 'Teeth, throat, and bowels are objectified hunger; the organs of generation are objectified sexual desire.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological/etiological explanations do not negate philosophical truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Physiological (etiological) accounts of bodily functions explain temporal/causal sequences but do not invalidate the philosophical truth that voluntary motion is manifestation of will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule for interpreting scientific accounts: even if physiology explains muscle movements causally, 'this would never invalidate the immediately certain truth that every voluntary motion... is the manifestation of an act of will.' Etiology gives positions in time/space but not inner nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate cause, stimulus, and motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 'cause' narrowly (proportional, reciprocal reaction; mechanics/chemistry), 'stimulus' (non-proportional effects on organised bodies), and 'motive' (idea-driven cause of volition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational criteria: causes allow measurement/proportion of effect; stimuli do not produce proportional reaction and are typical for organic processes; motives are ideas that determine actions under knowledge. Use these definitions to classify phenomena and their relation to will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulus as intermediary between cause and motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat stimulus as the mean between motive (knowledge-guided) and cause (purely mechanical), varying by case closer to one pole or the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when analyzing bodily/organismic functions (e.g., sap rising, pupil contraction, erections). Example: 'The stimulus holds the mean, forms the transition between the motive... and the cause in the narrowest sense.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise will in animals, plants, and unorganised nature by analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend recognition of will beyond humans to animals, plants, and even inorganic forces by observing analogous purposive or persistent tendencies (instinct, growth, crystal formation, magnetism, gravitation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical signs to attribute will: purposive regularity, persistent directional tendencies, increase of 'desire' by obstacles, precise formation (crystallisation), attraction/repulsion in chemistry. The passage: 'it will require no great effort of the imagination to recognise... our own nature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Will as thing-in-itself lies outside forms of the phenomenal (time, space, causality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The will as thing-in-itself is free from the forms of the phenomenal world (not subject to time, space, multiplicity or the principle of sufficient reason).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical implication: do not ascribe to the thing-in-itself the phenomenal categories; treat time and space as 'principium individuationis' that apply only to appearances. 'The will as a thing-in-itself lies outside the province of the principle of sufficient reason... and is consequently completely groundless.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile uncaused will with necessary manifestation
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the will itself is uncaused (groundless), its manifestations (phenomena) are subordinated to necessity and the principle of sufficient reason; actions therefore appear necessary although will-in-itself is uncaused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply to debates on freedom: self-consciousness gives illusion of absolute freedom, but 'every individual action follows with strict necessity from the effect of the motive upon the character.' Ethical and empirical consequences follow; treat freedom as misconstrued at phenomenal level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of extension by identity-in-difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical method: recognise identity across different phenomena (the same will in different manifestations) and difference within similar phenomena (degrees/grades of manifestation) to form the extended concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Plato-style 'knowledge of the identical in different phenomena' to justify extending 'will' beyond its human species: 'Knowledge of the identical in different phenomena, and of difference in similar phenomena, is... a sine qua non of philosophy.' Beware those who cannot extend the concept and therefore misunderstand.
